title: A/B testing with a permutation test
summary: Is the new version really better, or did we get lucky?

steps.title: Experiments beat observation
body: In an **A/B test** you **randomly** split users into two groups, show group A the current page and group B the new one, and measure a metric decided in advance (say, the conversion rate). Randomisation balances every confounder between the groups, so a real difference can be put down to the change.
But groups always differ a little by chance. The question becomes: *if the change did nothing* (the **null hypothesis**), how surprising would a difference this big be?

steps.explain: With 0/1 outcomes, the mean is the conversion rate. B converts 50% against A's 30%: 20 points more, a relative lift of 67%. With only 10 users each, that could easily be luck.

steps.title: The permutation test
body: If the change did nothing, the labels "A" and "B" are meaningless: any user could have been in either group. So:
2. pool all values, **shuffle** them, split into fake groups of the original sizes, compute the difference;
4. the **p-value** is the share of shuffled differences at least as extreme as the observed one: `np.mean(np.abs(diffs) >= abs(observed))` (two-sided).
A small p-value (commonly below 0.05) says "a gap this big rarely happens by chance alone".

steps.prompt: Arrange one round of the permutation test.

steps.title: Permutation test
prompt: Write `perm_test(a, b, rng, reps=5000)` returning the **two-sided** p-value (a plain float rounded to 4 decimals) for the difference in means `b.mean() - a.mean()`, using `rng.permutation` on the pooled values for each repetition.
The tests check that identical groups give p = 1.0, clearly different groups give a tiny p, and the result is between 0 and 1.
steps.starter:
import numpy as np


def perm_test(a, b, rng, reps=5000):
    a, b = np.asarray(a, dtype=float), np.asarray(b, dtype=float)
    ...
solution: a, b = np.asarray(a, dtype=float), np.asarray(b, dtype=float)
hints: Pool with `np.concatenate([a, b])`; each round `s = rng.permutation(pooled)`.
template: Dojo.eq("identical groups give p = 1.0", 1.0, perm_test([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 2, 3, 4], _rng, reps=500))
Dojo.check("a big gap gives a tiny p-value", _p < 0.01, f"p = {_p}")
Dojo.check("no real difference gives a large p-value", _q > 0.1, f"p = {_q}")
Dojo.check("p is a plain float", type(_q) is float, type(_q).__name__)

steps.prompt: An A/B test reports p = 0.03. What does that mean?
options: If the change had no effect, a difference at least this large would show up about 3% of the time by chance
There is a 3% chance the new version is better
There is a 97% chance the new version is better
The new version improves conversion by 3%
steps.explain: A p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about the size of the effect.

items: Choose the metric and sample size before starting
Randomly assign users to A or B
Check the p-value every hour and stop as soon as it dips below 0.05
Test 20 metrics and report the one that came out significant
Report the size of the effect with an interval, not just p
Put all mobile users in B because B is the mobile redesign
steps.explain: Peeking and testing many metrics both inflate false positives: with enough looks, chance alone eventually crosses 0.05. Non-random assignment brings confounders back.

steps.title: Make the call
prompt: - `"keep A"` when `p < alpha` and `lift < 0` (B is significantly worse);
- `"too small to matter"` when `p < alpha` but `0 <= lift < min_lift`;
Significance is not the same as importance, which is why there is a minimum lift.
hints: Handle `p >= alpha` first and return early.
template: Dojo.eq("significant but tiny", "too small to matter", decide(0.02, 0.005))

steps.title: The full A/B report
prompt: An experiment's results are in a DataFrame with columns `group` (`"A"` or `"B"`) and `converted` (0 or 1). Write `ab_report(df, rng)` that returns a dict:
- `"lift"`: relative lift `(rate_b - rate_a) / rate_a` rounded to 3 (from the unrounded rates);
- `"p"`: the two-sided permutation p-value (difference in means, 5000 shuffles with `rng.permutation`), rounded to 4;
Write `decide` again (or a helper of your own) in this step. Use plain Python floats.
